title: The Wild Thornberrys
full_review:
Based on the Nickelodeon cable channel's animated TV series, "The Wild Thornberrys Movie" (Paramount) makes a pleasant leap from small to big screen with a tame adventure that is family friendly to all but the tiniest of tots.

Mom and dad Thornberry (voices of Jodi Carlisle and Tim Curry) are nature documentary filmmakers on Africa's Serengeti Plain. Their 12-year-old, Eliza (voice of Lacey Chabert), harbors a secret she must keep or she'll lose it: that she can converse with animals. This especially endears her to her pet chimp, Darwin (voice of Tom Kane), but her impatient teen sister, Debbie (voice of Danielle Harris), just thinks Eliza's weird.

One day Eliza is off racing a trio of chatty cheetah cubs when nasty poachers swoop down in a helicopter and snatch one. Eliza is nearly injured, prompting her proper British grandmother (voice of Lynn Redgrave) to take Eliza back to England and a safe boarding school. Frisky Darwin manages to conceal himself in the luggage but soon causes food-fight pandemonium when he tries to pass himself off as a new student.

Eliza realizes she should go back and try to rescue the kidnapped cub. Once returned, she is befriended by a conservationist couple (voices of Marisa Tomei and Rupert Everett) while her sister gets sidetracked on a misadventure until a friendly native (voice of Obba Babatunde) comes to her aid.

Meanwhile, Eliza finds the captured cubs and discovers an even worse plot to kill an entire herd of elephants. What's more, the poachers snatch her sister, and the only way she can save her is to reveal her secret and lose her magical power.

As directed by Jeff McGrath and Cathy Malkasian, the full-length cartoon maintains a sprightly tone as spunky Eliza learns resourcefulness and the importance of family ties. And her sister's character, who at first comes off as annoyingly self-centered, is gradually revealed as simply sassy. Darwin's monkey business keeps the movie moving briskly, and the characters are, overall, a likeable lot.

However, the animation seldom reaches beyond standard TV quality. There are only occasional brief bursts of beauty and depth as if the film is trying for a "Lion King" feeling, but that's way out of their depth here. The sound, both music and sound effects, is quite good and the sprinkling of songs pleasing if not memorable. All in all, the Thornberrys are a nice family you wouldn't mind keeping company with for a little over an hour. The menace, while not intense, may be a bit too much for the more sensitive among the under-8 set.

Despite occasional mild peril, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
